images.title: File:Arkose (Fountain Formation, Pennsylvanian to Permian; Colorado, USA) 1.jpg
images.author: James St. John
images.description:
Arkose from the Pennsylvanian of Colorado, USA. (public display, Garden of the Gods visitor center, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA)
Arkose is a siliciclastic sedimentary rock dominated by clasts of pinkish-orangish colored potassium feldspar.  Arkose can be sandstone (~all sand-sized grains) or breccia (poorly sorted, with angular pebbles).
The sample seen here is an arkosic breccia from a thick, Pennsylvanian- to Permian-aged unit in Colorado called the Fountain Formation.  It represents an ancient alluvial fan deposit, composed of poorly sorted clastic debris eroded from the Ancestral Rocky Mountains.  The type locality is exposures adjacent to Fountain Creek in the town of Manitou Springs in central Colorado.  The Fountain Formation there includes arkosic quartzose sandstones, conglomeratic sandstones, granulose sandstones, and breccias.  The rocks are muscovitic in part.
Stratigraphy: Fountain Formation, Pennsylvanian to Permian

Locality: unrecorded/undisclosed (but possibly from Garden of the Gods, Colorado Springs, Colorado, USA)

images.title: File:00014 11 cm sulfur gypsum.jpg
images.author: Siim Sepp (Sandatlas)
images.description: Sulfur (yellow) and gypsum (gray) forming a cap rock of salt dome. Sulfur is a product of bacterial activity. Salt dome contains anhydrite (calcium sulfate), especially in the upper parts (cap rock) because salt (NaCl) is more soluble and gets preferentially carried away by groundwater. Anhydrite becomes gypsum when hydrated. Salt domes are often associated with hydrocarbons (crude oil and natural gas) because salt domes are ideal structural traps which restrict the rise of hydrocarbons. These hydrocarbons are source of energy for bacteria who decompose anhydrite to form hydrogen sulfide, calcium carbonate and water: anhydrite (CaSO4) + CH4 (hydrocarbons) + bacteria = H2S (hydrogen sulfide) + limestone (CaCO3) + water. H2S reacts with oxygen to form elemental sulfur and water: 2H2S + O2 = 2S + 2H2O. So, this rock is a perfect illustration how the cap rock of a salt dome looks like which also contains crude oil or natural gas. The width of the specimen is 11 cm. images.title: File:Brannhult.jpg
images.author: Gräsmark
images.description: Brännhult quarry in Älmhult municipality, Småland, southern Sweden. Here a dyke of Pre-Neoproterozoic dolerite is quarried that cuts through a suite of Paleoproterozoic metagranitoid rocks (monzogranite, quartz monzonite, granodiorite, quartz monzodiorite). The rocks belong to the so-called Protogine Zone, a several kilometers wide shear zone between the Sveconorwegian domain and the Transscandinavian Igneous Belt of the Baltic Shield.[1][2]

images.title: File:Astrée rugueuse (Bolma rugosa) (Ifremer 00661-77267 - 31122).jpg
images.author: Sandrine Vaz
images.description: The rough starfish, also known as the Mediterranean turbo or turbo scarbre, is a gastropod mollusk of Mediterranean waters, which can also be found in the eastern Atlantic, on muddy and rocky bottoms rich in brown algae on which it feeds. It is recognizable by its turbinate shell (5 cm high by 6 to 8 cm wide on average) and its 7 convex towers, but especially by its calcareous operculum: dark on the inside, this operculum is orange-pink on the outside, and its shape is reminiscent of the human eye. This earned it the name "Saint Lucy's eye", and is considered a lucky charm. Astraea rugosa (Linnaeus, 1758) is also widely used in many classifications for this species.

images.title: File:Alcyon rouge (Alcyonium glomeratum) et éponge clione (Cliona celata) (Ifremer 00737-84925 - 41493).jpg
images.author: Olivier Dugornay
images.description: A planktivorous carnivore, the tentacles of the polyps of the red alcyon ( Alcyonium glomeratum ), equipped with stinging cells called cnidocysts, trap food particles from zooplankton. Alongside the cnidarian, a clione sponge ( Cliona celata ) called a suction cup sponge: the latter comes in 3 different forms (alpha, beta and gamma). In these images, it is a gamma form, recognizable by its yellow-orange color and its massive body (70 cm on average), hanging overhanging from the rock or substrate on which the sponge is attached. The gamma form is more widespread in the Atlantic. Its vernacular name is due to the multiple ostioles, visible in its gamma form, resembling groups of suction cups.

images.author: Olivier Dugornay (Ifremer)
images.description: Artificial collectors for the recruitment of slipper limpet, submerged in different places in the harbor of Brest. In these photographs, the surface to be sampled is delimited by quadrats. Many black brittle stars ( Ophiocomina nigra ) have also invaded the place, in one of these two photos. Recognizable by its oval, domed and very slightly spiraled shell, this mollusk is an invasive species that lives mainly in shallow and sheltered coastal environments. images.author: Pierre-Marie Epiney
images.description:
"La Suisse se situe en limite nord de l’aire de nidification du Bruant fou, dont le caractère thermophile le porte à occuper en priorité le sud du pays, et ponctuellement aussi le Jura et les Alpes septentrionales. Il apprécie les habitats ouverts et semi-ouverts exposés au midi, qui vont des parois rocheuses ou carrières aux forêts claires, jeunes stades boisés et vignobles. Les densités élevées sont réservées au Valais, Tessin et val Poschiavo GR, où les carrés kilométriques propices comptent régulièrement plus de 12 territoires. La majorité de la population se reproduit entre 800 et 2000 m, mais les nidifications aux altitudes record ont été prouvées à Zermatt VS 2300-2400 m.
Depuis 1993-1996, la présence du Bruant fou a pu être nouvellement établie dans nombre de carrés atlas, en particulier le long des Alpes du Nord et dans les Grisons. Si certains cas peuvent relever d’un effort de prospection accru, d’autres trahissent probablement de véritables installations. Dans le Jura, seules subsistent des données d’isolés dans les rares carrés encore occupés après les lourdes pertes subies dès les années 1970. Dans les Vosges et la Forêt-Noire, le Bruant fou a aussi beaucoup décliné.

Ensis siliqua Linnaeus, 1758 - giant razor clam (public display, Bailey-Matthews Shell Museum, Sanibel Island, Florida, USA)
Bivalves are bilaterally symmetrical molluscs having two calcareous, asymmetrical shells (valves) - they include the clams, oysters, and scallops.  In most bivalves, the two shells are mirror images of each other (the major exception is the oysters).  They occur in marine, estuarine, and freshwater environments.  Bivalves are also known as pelecypods and lamellibranchiates.
Bivalves are sessile, benthic organisms - they occur on or below substrates.  Most of them are filter-feeders, using siphons to bring in water, filter the water for tiny particles of food, then expel the used water.  The majority of bivalves are infaunal - they burrow into unlithified sediments.  In hard substrate environments, some forms make borings, in which the bivalve lives.  Some groups are hard substrate encrusters, using a mineral cement to attach to rocks, shells, or wood.
The fossil record of bivalves is Cambrian to Recent.  They are especially common in the post-Paleozoic fossil record.
